editorNote: The home-computer trade takes stock while owners put their machines to work, play and music.
morningLine: Commodore counts the cost; cassette users pick up speed.

lead.headline: Commodore earnings plunge 94%; home-computer boom faces its reckoning
lead.dek: Quarterly profit shrinks to $3.2 million as the industry searches for its next reason to buy.
body: Commodore’s latest figures have put a hard number on the cooling home-computer boom. Paul Richter reports in the February 1 Los Angeles Times that quarterly profit fell 94 percent to $3.2 million. Sales for the quarter ended December 31 declined 21 percent from a year earlier, to $338.7 million.

Inventory exceeded $400 million. The results included a $30 million pretax charge connected with product pricing; analysts said it provided for compensation to retailers facing a planned Commodore 64 price cut. Their expectation was a move from roughly $200 to $150—not a confirmed new price at every counter.

The C64 remains a formidable installed base: the report credits Commodore with sales of more than three million machines. Yet an industry built on rapid expansion now has to persuade families that a computer offers enough beyond the first burst of curiosity. A strong dollar also hurt the company, which put the revenue effect at $35 million compared with year-earlier exchange rates.

New machines offer hope, but promises are not deliveries. The report anticipates the Commodore 128 in the first half, while analysts float an April arrival and an $800–$1,000 price for Amiga. Atari’s recently demonstrated ST is another challenger. For owners of today’s machines, the more immediate story is what can be done with the equipment already on the desk.

stories.headline: TurboTape promises disk-like loading from ordinary Commodore cassettes
body: A cassette deck need not condemn a Commodore owner to a long wait. January COMPUTE! publishes Harrie De Ceukelaire’s TurboTape for the C64 and VIC-20, offering what the magazine calls disk-like loading from ordinary tape hardware.

The utility handles BASIC and machine-language programs without modifying the computer or recorder. Saved tapes can subsequently load at accelerated speed without first loading TurboTape. On the C64 the resident utility takes 642 bytes; the VIC version uses 639.

The VIC listing needs at least 8K expansion for entry, although the resulting utility can run in any VIC memory configuration. This is a January magazine type-in, not a newly announced release this week, and the speed comparison remains the magazine’s claim.

stories.headline: The C64 becomes a six-track music studio
body: The Commodore 64 can be more than a game machine or household ledger. Richard Mansfield’s January COMPUTE! review describes Sequential Circuits Music Sequencer, a $225 package joining the computer to a compatible synthesizer over MIDI.

Six recorded tracks can be edited, looped, copied, erased or transposed separately. Tempo can change without changing pitch, and as many as eight sequences can be chained into a song and saved. Tape or disk storage is recommended alongside the required computer and synthesizer.

Timing autocorrection offers selectable resolutions, but six tracks do not mean every connected instrument produces six different sounds at once. The review distinguishes ordinary synthesizer limits from the Six-Trak’s multivoice capability with expansion software.

stories.headline: JTERM’s new version brings 1200-bps access to Atari bulletin-board callers
body: Atari callers have a fresh reason to examine their terminal software. Frank C. Jones’s JTERM 3.8, published in January COMPUTE!, adds 1200-bps modem support while retaining 300-bps operation. It requires at least 32K RAM and an Atari 850 Interface Module or equivalent.

Jones describes donating his terminal to a Washington, D.C. Atari user-group bulletin board operated by Frank Huband. Suggestions and complaints from callers helped shape its development—an example of software improving through a working community rather than a sealed retail box.

The BASIC and machine-language terminal serves bulletin boards, commercial information services, mainframe connections and file transfers. Jones reports extensive use, but his account is not an independently measured census of callers.

computerItems.title: Paratrooper
computerItems.summary: John Goetz’s January COMPUTE! type-in game gives ten parachutists per round, with wind, weight and altitude determining landing. Three pads score 25, 50 and 75 points; versions cover TI-99/4A, C64, VIC-20, Atari, Apple, IBM PC, PCjr, Plus/4 and Commodore 16. Publication timing, not a commercial release date.

briefs.summary: February 1 LA Times cites Electronics Industries Association estimates of 7.3 million VCRs sold in 1984, up 78% from 4.1 million in 1983. This is retrospective market context, not a weekly gadget launch.

worldAnchor.headline: Stars assemble to record famine-relief song
worldAnchor.summary: The We Are the World recording session took place January 28, 1985, bringing artists together for African famine relief. The single was not yet released; do not place its March release or later sales in the week’s news.

curiosity.detail: The January type-in occupies only 642 bytes on the C64; accelerated saved tapes can reload without the utility preinstalled. Disk-like performance is the magazine’s claim, not a fresh benchmark.
